poems.text: If anyone is afraid of hanging himself, but wants to die, let him drink cold water from Hierapolis.

poems.title: Book IX, 399
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thy mind, by its sweet light, conquered the sun, ever flashing forth soft brilliance of wisdom to illuminate mortals, a pleasant and painless splendour.

poems.title: Book IX, 402: On Pompey the Great
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: In what sore need of a tomb stood he who possessed abundant temples !

poems.title: Book IX, 431: On a Thief who found a Gold Sword
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I too love gold, and I shrink from hostile Ares.

poems.title: Book IX, 436: An Inscription from Syracuse
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The votive offerings to Apollo were old, but as for the base it is in one case twenty, in another seven, in another twelve, and in this last case two hundred years later; for so the figures work out when counted.

poems.title: Book IX, 448: Homer’s Question
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Fishermen from Arcadia, what have we? The Answer We left what we caught and carry what we did not catch.

poems.title: Book IX, 449: What Love would say if he were in love
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who is this that overcame fire by fire, who quenched a torch with a torch? Who drew another bow against mine? A new Love by my might contends on equal terms with Love.

poems.title: Book IX, 451: What Philomela would say to her Sister Procne
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thy wicked husband shut me up, ill-fated that I am, alone in a deep cave, and took my maidenhead. An abominable present he made me on this my calamitous marriage, cutting off my tongue and quenching Greek speech in me.

poems.title: Book IX, 452: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thy sister Philomela, Procne, wishes thee well if this be well-wishing. Let the robe tell thee the suffering of my heart which savage Tereus inflicted on me. Shutting me up, luckless maid, in the shepherd’s fold, he deprived me first of virginity and next of speech.

poems.title: Book IX, 454: What Calliope would say to George
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This man, not Zeus, is my true father.

poems.title: Book IX, 455: What Apollo would say about Homer
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The song is mine, but divine Homer wrote it down.

poems.title: Book IX, 456: Pasiphae to Love
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If thou hast taught me to love a bull that roams over the mountains, teach me to low so that Imay call my dear husband.

poems.title: Book IX, 457: What Achilles would say if Agamemnon were wounded
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou knowest now, Agamemnon, my man-destroying wrath; thou knowest how great is Hector’s strength in hand-to-hand combat. For all have now perished owing to thy insult fraught with disaster, and a greater woe, worse than death, has come upon thee. Thou sufferest the evil and intolerable sorrow due to thy folly, who wast the defence in battle of all the Greeks.

poems.title: Book IX, 458: What Ulysses would say on landing in Ithaca
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hail, Ithaca! After all my labours and the bitter woes of the sea, right glad am I to reach thy soil, in hope to see Laertes and my wife and glorious only son. Love of thee soothed my heart; I myself know that “nothing is sweeter than a man’s country and his parents.”

poems.title: Book IX, 459: What Achilles would say on seeing Ulysses in Hades
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Or a truth Odysseus is the most resourceful of men. Alive he looks on what it is not allowed to see, the infernal recesses and the bitter pains of the dead. How did he venture to leave the holy light? Did some necessity bring him here against his will? Odysseus never has his fill of cunning devices on earth, on the sea, and among the dead.

poems.title: Book IX, 460: What Achilles would have said when he saw the Armour lying before him
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Mother, thou bringest to thy valiant son this armour, a glorious gift such as no man ever looked on. Now I know that Pallas arms my hand against Hector, and prepares disgrace and death for the Trojans.

poems.title: Book IX, 461: What Pyrrhus would say on entering Troy
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: ‘The labour of my noble father was not completed, but I have come, preparing slaughter for all the Trojans ; for I glory more exceedingly in my valour, and my might is capable of destroying in battle King Priam and all that Achilles left alive. The warlike city of Troy will I sack, and my spear shall complete the ten years’ labour of the Greeks.

poems.title: Book IX, 462: What Deidamia would say when Pyrrhus had sacked Troy
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou hast made to cease all the heavy woe of my heart for the fate of thy father Achilles, whom mournful Troy slew. To the Greeks who were eager for it thou hast given the undying glory which the ten years of war could not accomplish for the whole host of the Danai.

poems.title: Book IX, 463: What Hector would say when he saw Achilles in the Armour
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Athena in her wrath has again clothed the son of Peleus in immortal mail. Some worse woe shall befall the unhappy Trojans and Hector and his father, since the goddess gave this man this armour.

poems.title: Book IX, 464: What Paris would say when Menelaus was wounded
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Out on you all, ye craven Argives! Menelaus is dead now and gives me greater glory.

poems.title: Book IX, 465: What Althaea, entreating Meleager, would say
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: My son, thou forgettest thy family and heedest not thy country’s fate. Thou hast cast aside thy strong sword, putting Oeneus and Calydon and her people to shame.

poems.title: Book IX, 466: What Alcestis would say when Admetus yoked a Lion and Boar to his Chariot
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Great deeds of valour crowned thy chariot, and with excellently composed wedding hymns men celebrate thy bride.

poems.title: Book IX, 467: What Peleus would say on hearing that Achilles absented himself from the Battle
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Ye peaks of Pelias, who nursed him, tell my son, whom Chiron taught to be first in battle, to cast off his wrath and fatal enmity to the Greeks.

poems.title: Book IX, 468: What Hera would say when Heracles was deified
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thy father, Heracles, has well rewarded thy valiant toil, since labour can bring to men unsurpassable renown after an infinite round of labours.

poems.title: Book IX, 469: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Labour and immense toil procured thee the favour of occupying a blessed seat that no man reached before thee.

poems.title: Book IX, 470: What Achilles would say to reconcile Ajax with Ulysses
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: It is not permitted to nourish ill-will among the dead. Now thou hast escaped the sorrows of earth, love thy friend; for Odysseus did not sin against thee of his own will, but the strong hand of Athena killed thee, and Father Zeus, and Fate, and the Erinys that walks in darkness. Would that divine Thetis had cast the armour into the salt depths of the sea, stilling the strife of thy heart.

poems.title: Book IX, 471: What Nestor would say on learning of Ulysses’ return
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The good man has escaped the merciless sea, and after toil has reached his fatherland, and he must be my better, as he has become well acquainted with cities and customs and the minds of men.

poems.title: Book IX, 472: On Ulysses
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: It was after much toil that long-suffering Odysseus came home; yet Odysseus, the sacker of cities, surely has great fame on land and sea among men of future times.

poems.title: Book IX, 473: What Agamemnon would say when Achilles was armed
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Beetling Ilion is fallen, and God has given it a prey to the Greeks now that Achilles has cast off his wrath and arms his murderous hands.

poems.title: Book IX, 474: What Idothea would say on seeing Helen in Pharos
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I pity thy beauty, since thou art the child of Zeus, For I see a god-nourished form, and verily thou wast the cause of the ten years’ war between Greeks and Trojans. Where is the help of aegis-bearing Zeus thy father? But go soon on thy way, making, by the kindness of Idothea, a safe voyage home over the back of the cruel sea.

poems.title: Book IX, 475: What Helen would say on seeing the Combat between Paris and Menelaus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Ye warlike kings of Europe and Asia, for both of you it stands upon a razor’s edge, which of you long-suffering men shall take unhappy me to wife. Let Father Zeus decide, but without Aphrodite’s help, lest another thief of wedded women steal me, a disgrace to Greece.

poems.title: Book IX, 476: What Hector would say when Patroclus could not lift the Spear of Achilles
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thy weakness has defrauded Hector, for thou bringest me defective spoils.

poems.title: Book IX, 477: What Thetis would say when Telephus was tripped up by the vine
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Vine, what shall I do when Daphnaean Apollo lays low my vine-branch by the arrow of Alexander?

poems.title: Book IX, 478: What Priam would say when Helen advised the Greeks how to take Troy
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Splendid is the gift thou offerest thy country.

poems.title: Book IX, 479: What Perseus would say after slaying the Monster, when Andromeda refused him
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The cruel fetters of the rock have turned thy heart to stone, and now let the eye of Medusa turn thy body, too, to stone.

poems.title: Book IX, 480: What Hippodamia would say after the Death of Ocenomaus if Pelops refused to marry her
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Hippodamia. Thou turnest thy back on me now thou hast liberty to enjoy me. Pelops. Yea, for Love does not go hand in hand with such liberty. Love walks in another path.

poems.title: Book IX, 483: On a Child who was poisoned by Peach Kernels
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: From the murderous Persians Perseus brought back a murderous fruit which caused the death of Theognostus’ child.

poems.title: Book IX, 492: On a Soldier’s Arms
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Together lay shield and sword, arrows, cuirass, helmet, horse.

poems.title: Book IX, 493
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Another shield, bow and arrows, helmet, sword, strong spear.

poems.title: Book IX, 494
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Another Arrow, bow, shield, helmet, spear, sword, cuirass.

poems.title: Book IX, 495: Spoken by Agamemnon
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Dwellers in Greece, noble chieftains, place no trust any longer in perfidious women. A woman overcame me, whom my foe Hector slew not.

poems.title: Book IX, 498: On a Persian
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Bury not the unburied ; leave him to be the prey of dogs. Earth, the mother of all, will not receive the man who defiles the bed of his mother.

poems.title: Book IX, 499
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Grey Time goes along in silence, but as he creeps by he steals the voices of speaking men. Himself unseen, he makes the seen unseen and brings the unseen to light. O undetermined end of the life of men who day by day advance towards the dark!

poems.title: Book IX, 500
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No longer call the living heirs, but call the dead heirs. The dead are now heirs, and gain a great inheritance, departure from this wretched life.

poems.title: Book IX, 501: On an Earthquake
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The dead used to leave the city alive behind them, but we living now carry the city to her grave.

poems.title: Book IX, 504: On the Muses
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Calliope discovered the art of heroic verse; Clio the sweet music of the lyre which accompanies the dance; Euterpe the sonorous voice of the tragic chorus; Melpomene found for mortals the honeytoned barbitos, and charming Terpsichore gave us the artful flute; Erato invented cheering hymns to the gods; learned Polymnia the joys of the dance; Urania discovered the pole and the dance of the stars of heaven, and Thalia the plots and good moral teaching of comedy.

poems.title: Book IX, 505: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The painter never saw Terpsichore, but owing to his art the image deceives our eyes by its truth. If, my friend, you ever hear the lyre that cheers the heart, admire Erato, who possesses such skill. Euterpe shrills on perforated reeds, scattering on them and forcing through them the spirit of the skilled bee. I, Thalia, am concerned with comic verse, and I present in play, on the scene that loves the castanets, the actions of immoral people. Look on the image of thy wisdom; for thy heart should conceive Calliope’s image to be wisdom. I, Clio, dwell by the laurelled tripods of Phoebus, the Muse of prophecy and history. I, Urania, through calculations revealed by God, teach the recurring necessity of the stars’ motions. Look on Melpomene, skilled in lovely eloquence, giving force to brazen-voiced epic song. I, Polymnia, am silent, but speak through the entrancing motions of my hands, conveying by my gestures a speaking silence.

poems.title: Book IX, 510
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Critonianus married me, Solon begat me, my name was Meltine, I was moulded by the hands of my husband.

poems.title: Book IX, 511
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Asclepios ordered me in his kindness to adorn his grey locks with gold, and I gladly did it, since he deemed this service on my part to be pleasing to him.

poems.title: Book IX, 512: On a Book
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Teacher of the ruler of Rome, be gracious to me, accepting kindly the mysteries of the book of Protus, the deep words revealed by the pen of Philoponus.‘

poems.title: Book IX, 514
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am the god who is always chanted in the chambers of brides, and Menis, the comic actor, polished me well for the wedding of newly-married Procilla, and sent me with this prayer: “Go, Hymenaeus, in friendly wise, to both bride and bridegroom.”

poems.title: Book IX, 515
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Graces are three, and thou art one born for these three, that the Graces may have a Grace.

poems.title: Book IX, 520: On Alcaeus (probably by his enemy King Philip)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is the tomb of Alcaeus who was killed by the broad-leaved daughter of earth, the radish, punisher of adulterers.

poems.title: Book IX, 521: The Muses to Sappho
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No little fame, Sappho, did Fate grant thee on the day thou didst first see the sun. For we consented that thy utterances should be immortal, and the Father of all, the Thunderer, approved. All men shall sing thee, and thou shalt not lack glorious report.

poems.title: Book IX, 522
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Iliad, thou great work, and Odyssey, chaste poem, that hast made Ithaca Troy’s equal, make me, the old man, grow in eternal youth; for from your lips flows the Siren song of Homer.

poems.title: Book IX, 523
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Calliope, eloquent goddess of Helicon the pasture of bees, bear me a second Homer, since a second Achilles has come.

poems.title: Book IX, 524
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A Hymn to Dionysus (containing his Epithets in Alphabetical Order) Ler us chant the king who loves the call of Euhoe, the King Eiraphiotes, Tender-haired, rustic, much besung, fair of form, Boeotian, Bromius, reveller, with vine-leaves in his hair, Merry, productive, slayer of giants, the laugher, Son of Zeus, twice-born, son of the Dithyramb, Dionysus, Euius, with lovely locks, rich in vines, awaker of revels, Jealous, very wrathful, envious, bestower of envy, Gentle, sweet drinker, sweet-voiced, cozener, Thracian, thyrsus-bearing, boon-companion, lion-hearted, Slayer of Indians, desirable, twiner of violets, hiercphant, Reveller, horned, ivy-crowned, noisy, Lydian, lord of the wine-press, dispeller of care, Healer of sorrow, mystic, frenzied, giver of wine, thousand-shaped, God of the night, shepherd-god, fawn-like, clothed in fawn-skin, Spear-thrower, common to all, giver of guests, yellowhaired, Prone to anger, stout of heart, lover of the mountain shade, wanderer on the mountains, Deep drinker, wanderer, wearer of many garlands, constant reveller, Mind-breaker, slender, wrinkled, clad in sheep-skin, Leaper, satyr, son of Semele, Jovial, bull-faced, slayer of Tyrrhenians, swift to wrath, Chaser of sleep, liquid, hymeneal, dweller in the woods, Mad for wild beasts, terrible, laughter-loving, wanderer, ’ Golden-horned, graceful, relaxer of the mind, goldenfilleted, Disturber of the soul, liar, bent on noise, tearer of the soul, Seasonable, eater of raw flesh, nurtured on the mountains, making clamour on the mountains. Let us chant the King who loves the call of Euhoe, the King Eiraphiotes.

poems.title: Book IX, 525: A similar Hymn to Apollo
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Let us hymn Paean the great god, Apollo ; Immortal, gloriously formed, unshorn, soft-haired, Stern-hearted, king, delighting in arrows, giver of life Joyous, laughing, slayer of giants, sweet-hearted, Son of Zeus, slayer of the dragon, lover of the laurel, Sweet of speech, of ample might, far-shooter, giver of hope, Creator of animals, divine, Jove-minded, giver of zeal, Mild, sweet-spoken, sweet-hearted, gentle-handed, Slayer of beasts, blooming, charmer of the spirit, soft-speaking, a i Shooter of arrows, desirable, healer, charioteer, Weaver of the world, Clarian, strong-hearted, father of fruits, Son of Leto, pleasant, delighting in the lyre, resplendent, Lord of the mysteries, prophet, magnanimous, thousand-shaped, Lover of the bow-string, wise, stiller of grief, sober, Lover of community, common to all, taking thought for all, benefactor of all, Blessed, making blessed, Olympian, dweller on the hills, Gentle, all-seeing, sorrowless, giver of wealth, Saviour from trouble, rose-coloured, man-breaker, path-opener, Glittering, wise, father of light, saviour, Delighting in the dance, Titan, initiator, revered, Chanter of hymns, highest, stately, of the height, Phoebus, purifier, lover of garlands, cheerer of the spirit, Utterer of oracles, golden, golden-complexioned, golden-arrowed, Lover of the lyre, harper, hater of lies, giver of the soul, Swift-footed, swift-voiced, swift of vision, giver of seasons. Let us hymn Paean the great god, Apollo,

poems.title: Book IX, 527: Oracle from Herodotus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Lion, with long-suffering heart, bear the unbearable. No evil man shall escape punishment.

poems.title: Book IX, 529: On the Bed of a Harlot made of Laurel
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I who fled the bed of one, am made a bed for many.

poems.title: Book IX, 530: On an Unworthy Magistrate
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Fortune did not willingly give you advancement, but to show that her omnipotence reaches even as low as you.

poems.title: Book IX, 531: On the Isaurians
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: They run equal to the winds; hence their name.

poems.title: Book IX, 532: To a Pumpkin
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Tell me, pumpkin, why even so late as this the watery tribe of cucumbers and pumpkins has not appeared. The Pumpkins Reply Zeus rained heavily and flooded the fields, which still hide our race against our will.

poems.title: Book IX, 533: On a Beast-fighter who escaped by means of a Pole
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A man fixed a pole on the ground, and throwing himself into the air made a somersault, and with his nimble feet passed over the back of the beast that was rushing at him. It failed to catch him; the people applauded loudly and the man escaped.

poems.title: Book IX, 534: On Artemis
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Artemis, sweating, forbodes war.

poems.title: Book IX, 535
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Dionysus glories in ivy, Zeus in the aegis, the inhabitants of this city in their hospitality, and the city in her inhabitants.

poems.title: Book IX, 536: On the River Alpheius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Water in the sea travelled through water without getting wet.

poems.title: Book IX, 540
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Do not rapidly unfold to the end of the roll the book of Heraclitus the Ephesian. The path is very difficult, and all is mist and unilluminated darkness ; but if one initiated introduce you, it is clearer than the bright sun.

poems.title: Book IX, 571: On the Nine Lyric Poets
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Pindar screamed loud from Thebes, the Muse of Simonides breathed delight with her sweet-strained voice, Stesichorus and Ibycus shine, Aleman was sweet, and Bacchylides’ lips uttered dainty song, Persuasion attended on Anacreon, Lesbian Alcaeus sings varied strains on the Aeolian... But Sappho was not the ninth among men, but is tenth in the list of the lovely Muses.

poems.title: Book IX, 574
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I, roo, thrice unhappy Anaxis, carted along the burden of this weary life that is no life. Yet I did not pull it for long, but spurning from me this distraught life I went to Hades.

poems.title: Book IX, 580: On the Roman Months
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The consuls’ month is first, the second cuts the furrow, the third rouses the Italians to war, the fourth announces the rosy-fingered season of spring. I, May, am the mother of roses. I, June, bring white lilies. This, July, is the binder of sheaves. August’s wings make the Nile rise. This, September, is dear to Bacchus, rich in grapes. I, October, make honeyed wine, a delight for men. I, November, bring a joyful banquet to every man. I, December, teach men to play on the lyre and to awaken sleepers.

poems.title: Book IX, 581: On a Beast-fight in the Theatre
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: (The words are put in the mouth of the Emperor ) Bowman, lord of the Muses, far-shooter Phoebus, tell thy sister to arouse the mighty beasts just enough for them to touch men’s bodies lightly and make the people cry out for pleasure in holy tones. Let me not, who sit on the throne of Jove the Merciful, look upon a man’s death.

poems.title: Book IX, 582
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: These Armenian tribes and the doughty Iberian people, full of zeal for Christ, came willingly under the yoke, submitting themselves to the law of our invincible emperors.

poems.title: Book IX, 583: On Thucydides
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: My friend, if thou art learned, take me in thy hand; but if thou art ignorant of the Muses, cast away what thou canst not understand. I am not accessible to all, but the few admire Thucydides, son of Olorus, by birth an Athenian.

poems.title: Book IX, 584: On the Statue at Delphi of Eunomus the Lyre-player
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou knowest, Apollo, how I, Eunomus the Locrian, conquered Spartis, but I tell it for those who ask me. I was playing on the lyre an elaborate piece, and in the middle of it my plectron loosened one chord, and when the time came to strike the note I was ready to play, it did not convey the correct sound to the ear. Then of its own accord a cicada perched on the bridge of the lyre and supplied the deficiency of the harmony. I had struck six chords, and when I required the seventh I borrowed this cicada’s voice ; for the midday songster of the hillside adapted to my performance that pastoral air of his, and when he shrilled he combined with the lifeless chords to change the value of the phrase. Therefore I owe a debt of thanks to my partner in the duet, and wrought in bronze he sits on my lyre.

poems.title: Book IX, 585: On a Dish with a Relief of Venus and Loves
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Here are four Loves. One fits the garland to his mother’s brows, one has his lips at her bosom’s fountain, two play at her feet, and the robe covers the place that is next to the thighs of Aphrodite, otherwise wholly undraped.

poems.title: Book IX, 589: On a Statue of Hera suckling Heracles
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A true stepmother did the sculptor render. Therefore he added no milk to the breast that was not kindred.

poems.title: Book IX, 590: On a Group of Hephaestus, Athena, and Erechtheus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: “Art united that which Nature did not,” said the sculptor. “O mother without birth and bridegroom without marriage !”

poems.title: Book IX, 591: On a Group of Ares and Aphrodite
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The painter in the interior of the house painted Ares and Aphrodite embracing each other. The bright Sun, coming in through the window, stood in astonishment as he gazed on them both. Till when shall the heavy wrath of the Sun endure? He, would not banish his anger though it fell only on lifeless wax.

poems.title: Book IX, 592: On a Shield representing the Birth of Christ
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: How simple was the artist to engrave the birth of the Prince of Peace on a shield !

poems.title: Book IX, 593: On a Statue of Medea
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The inspired hand infused into the marble both pity and fury, and made the stone Medea, under the empire of his art, remember all her griefs.

poems.title: Book IX, 594: On a Picture of Socrates
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Painter, who hast reproduced the form of Socrates, would thou couldst have put his soul into the wax!

poems.title: Book IX, 595: On a Picture of Apelles
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Apelles painted himself in the picture.

poems.title: Book IX, 596: On a Picture of Chilon
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Sparta, glorious in war, gave birth to this Chilon, who was first in wisdom of the seven sages.

poems.title: Book IX, 601
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This passing fair statue did Aeximenes erect to Aphrodite, the protectress of all navigation. Hail, sovereign Cypris! and if thou givest gain and welcome wealth thou shalt learn that a ship is most ready to go shares.

poems.title: Book IX, 606
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Look at Cytherea whom Ares once loved, bathing here in the limpid stream. Look at her swimming, and fear not. It is not maiden Athena that you see, as Tiresias did.

poems.title: Book IX, 607
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Graces bathed here, and to reward the bath they gave to the water the brightness of their limbs.

poems.title: Book IX, 608
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Either such water gave birth to Cytherea, or Cytherea, by bathing in it, made the water such.

poems.title: Book IX, 609
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This bath is the playground of the Graces, for it only admits the Graces to sport within it.

poems.title: Book IX, 609a
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is really the Graces’ bath, for it cannot contain more than three.

poems.title: Book IX, 610
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is a little work, but beautiful to look on, like a rose in a garden or a violet in a basket of flowers.

poems.title: Book IX, 611
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: There is great charm in a little bath. Sweet love looks on those who bathe in the tiniest stream.

poems.title: Book IX, 612
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: As a myrtle has little leaves, but sweet-scented, so this bath is small, but dear.

poems.title: Book IX, 613: On the Bath of Maria
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Momus wept when he saw the bath of Maria, exclaiming : “I have to leave you unvisited, as I leave Maria.”

poems.title: Book IX, 615: On a Bath at Smyrna
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou building, who of mortals made thee, who wast formerly dim, rich in light for bathers, and who, cleaning away the smoky grime that befouled thee, brightened thee thus? It was wise Theodorus who in this truly, as in everything, showed the cleanness of his heart. He being the treasurer and father of the city’s possessions, did not stain his hands by gain derived from them. Mighty Christ, immortal God, keep by Thy hand this patriot out of the reach of misfortune.

poems.title: Book IX, 616
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Here once when the Graces bathed, little Eros stole their immortal raiment and went off with it, leaving them naked and ashamed to appear outside the door.

poems.title: Book IX, 617: On a too cold Bath
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who walled round a river, bathman? Who falsely styled this fountain a bath? ‘Aeolus, son of Hippotas, dear to the immortal gods,’! brought the winds here from their home. And why are these two planks placed here for the feet? Not for warmth, but for freezing. This is the place of Shivering and Frost-bite. Write thereon: “Bathe here in August, for the north wind blows ever within.”

poems.title: Book IX, 618: On a Bath in Byzantium
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The old story of the lotus-eaters ? is no falsehood. This bath confirms its truth. For if a man once bathe in these -pure waters he does not regret his country or desire his parents.

poems.title: Book IX, 621
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Such women as have desire to please (and ye all have) come here, and ye shall win brighter charms. She who has a husband will give her husband pleasure, and the unmarried girl will stir many to offer her marriage. And she who makes her living by her body, if she bathe here, will have swarms of lovers at her door.

poems.title: Book IX, 622
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If sweet desire for thy wedded wife possess thee, bathe here, and thou shalt appear to her brighter. Or if lust drive thee to mercenary and depraved women, bathe here, and thou shalt be paid instead of paying.

poems.title: Book IX, 632: On other Hot Baths
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Where Earth in her inmost recesses has perpetual fire and boils with hidden flames, the hot vapour, ascending to the air owing to the pressure from below, belches forth streams of water heated by fire.

poems.title: Book IX, 634
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Graces swore by the radiant lord of light rather to dwell here than with Cypris.

poems.title: Book IX, 635
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This bath bears the name of the leafy laurel.

poems.title: Book IX, 636
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: It was on seeing this bath that sagest Homer said: “Allaying grief and anger, bringing oblivion of all evil.”

poems.title: Book IX, 637
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: After bathing her divine limbs here, Cypris straightway showed herself to Alexander, and carried off the prize of the apple.

poems.title: Book IX, 638
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The three Graces of Orchomenus made the bath, and therefore it has not room for four.

poems.title: Book IX, 639
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Cypris, Love, the Graces, the Nymphs, Dionysus, and Apollo swore to each other to dwell here.

poems.title: Book IX, 640
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The immortals bathe when the bath is first opened, at the fifth hour the demi-gods, and later all the rubbish,

poems.title: Book IX, 646: On the Pontic Heraclea
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If you know of another city with the same name, Heraclea, know that I, the Pontic one, do not rank beneath it.

poems.title: Book IX, 647: On Rome
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Rome, queen of the world, thy fame shall never perish, for Victory, being wingless, cannot fly from thee.

poems.title: Book IX, 655: On the Banqueting Hall of Magnaura
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This house was diligently completed by the emperors, on whom the Cross bestowed a beneficent power, Heraclius and his son Constantine.

poems.title: Book IX, 656: On the House called Chalce in the Palace built by Anastasius
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am the house of Anastasius, the emperor, slayer of tyrants, and I alone far excel all cities of the Earth. I am a cause of wonder to all, since the architects, seeing my height, length, and vast breadth, were minded to leave the huge pile unroofed; but skilled Aetherius, the most eminent master of that laborious art, devised my shape, laying the first-fruits of his toil before our stainless emperor. Therefore, stretching on all sides my vast bulk, I surpass the celebrated wonders of the Italian land. Beauty of the Capitolian hall, give place to thy betters, even though thy golden roof dazzles the eye. Hide, Pergamus, thy splendid ornament, the grove of Rufinus, narrow now beside the halls of this limitless palace ; and thou, Cyzicus, no longer sing of thy noble temple of Hadrian standing fast on the long cliff. The pyramids are not capable of vying with me, or the colossus, or the Pharus; I alone surpass a great legion of buildings. My prince himself, after his victory over the Isaurians, completed me, the house of the Dawn, shining with gold, on all sides exposed to the breezes of the four winds.

poems.title: Book IX, 660: On the Basilica of the Schools in Constantinople
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am a place dedicated to Law. Here gushes forth an abundant fount of Roman Jurisprudence which runs perennially for all, and gives its whole stream to the youth here assembled.

poems.title: Book IX, 666: On a Garden called Eros
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Eros is not big, but he is pretty. So I am not great among gardens, but am full of charm.

poems.title: Book IX, 670: On a Mole in Smyrna on which there was a Cistern
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A. who made the deep dry land, who amid the surges built out of marble a shore washed on both sides by the sea? And who enabled the sailors to obtain water in the midst of the waves, drawing it with their hands even from the deck? Jb. This resourceful man, noble Venetius, who surpassed Theseus and Pelops by his creations.

poems.title: Book IX, 671: On a Lighthouse in the same City
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A. who executed so great a work? What is his city and what his office? 8B. Ambrosius of Mylasa, the proconsul, built the lighthouse.

poems.title: Book IX, 672: On the same City
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Though thou journeyest over the sea-bound circle of the whole dry land, thou shalt nowhere see a place superior to this which renowned Ioannes, glorifying her the queen of all this land, has made so admirable ; for from the sea itself! he won unceasing delight for Homer’s city.

poems.title: Book IX, 673: On a Place in the same City
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Asclepius did this work, too, for Hippolyta.

poems.title: Book IX, 674: In the Pharos at Alexandria
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am the tower that helps straying mariners, lighting up the blaze of Poseidon’s comforting torch. Ammonius, who is the father of our emperor,’ re-erected me by his labour when, borne down by the loud-roaring gales, I was about to fall. To him the sailors, escaped from the wild waves, lift up their hands as to the glorious Earth-shaker.

poems.title: Book IX, 675: On the Lighthouse at Smyrna
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Sail to me fearlessly, ye mariners, no longer dreading the rayless gloom of the night. For all wanderers burns my far-flashing torch, keeping alive the memory of my builders the Asclepiadae.

poems.title: Book IX, 676: On a Fountain in the Asiatic Mount Olympus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I yield to the Nymphs of Prusa, and salute, too, those of the Pythian waters as my superiors. But let the whole company of Naiads after Pythia and after Prusa give way to my Nymphs.

poems.title: Book IX, 678: On a Village near Smyrna
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: What a great and laborious work is this, too, that thou hast achieved, Agaclides, gaining great glory by thy daring! Thou hast enriched this parched land of the ancient Nymph Bassa with water and baths.

poems.title: Book IX, 679: On an Aqueduct at Assus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: All cities worship Axiochus, for, on his progress, like a god he has healed the ills of each. Especially on rugged Assus did he bestow running water, cutting through the hard face of many rocks. No longer run off to a distance, all ye travellers. I overflow with the cold water of Axiochus.

poems.title: Book IX, 680: On a Sea-side Garden at Antioch in which was a Bath
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou seest in me the three Graces, stranger. Poseidon wrought the one from the neighbouring sea, the second is the work of my garden rich in produce, and the remaining one is supplied by this bath.

poems.title: Book IX, 682: On the Obelisk in the Hippodrome
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: It was only the Emperor Theodosius who under-took to raise the four-sided column which had ever lain a burden on the earth. He committed the task to Proclus, and so great a column stood erect in thirty-two days.

poems.title: Book IX, 683: On Alpheus and Arethusa
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Alpheus is a male water, Arethusa a female, and Love accomplished their marriage by mixing the waters.

poems.title: Book IX, 684: On the Fountain on the Island Taphos
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am the fountain Nychea, daughter of Ocean and Tethys, for so the Teleboae named me. I pour forth a bath for the Nymphs and health for mortals. It was Pterelas, the son of Ares, who placed me here.

poems.title: Book IX, 685: On Camarina the Sicilian Lake
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Move not Camarina, for it is best unmoved, lest, if thou move it, thou make the lesser greater.

poems.title: Book IX, 686: On the Eastern Gate of Thessalonica
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Exult in thy heart, stranger, when thou seest above the gate the prefect Basil, destroyer of the valour of insolent Babylon and light of incorrupt justice. Thou goest to the place of good government, the mother of excellent sons. Thou hast no need to fear the barbarian or sodomites. The Spartan for a wall has his arms, and thou a royal statue (or the statue of Basil.)

poems.title: Book IX, 687: On a Painting
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I wo painted the form would fain have painted also the character, but the limits of art checked my eagerness. Call me eloquent Alexander, my friend.

poems.title: Book IX, 688: On the Gate of Argos
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This gate, built of polished stone, both an ornament for Argos and an object of admiration for travellers, was erected by Cleadas, the husband of gentle and noble Clea. He was the excellent hierophant of the sanctuary of Lerna, and enjoyed the generosity of powerful monarchs.

poems.title: Book IX, 689: On the Gate of Eugenius in Constantinople
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This Julian who built the walls that protect the city erected the trophy in memory of his vigilance. He studied rather to slay his enemies at a distance than to stir up war before the city.

poems.title: Book IX, 690: On the Gate called Xylocircus at Constantinople
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Theodosius ‘the emperor and Constantine, prefect of the East, built this wall in sixty days.

poems.title: Book IX, 691: On the Gate of Rhesius at Constantinople
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: In sixty days Constantine the prefect built this strengthening wall for his sceptred sovereign.

poems.title: Book IX, 692: On some Building
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is the work of Vivianus, of whom East and West sing with honour because of his just government.

poems.title: Book IX, 693: On a Temple of Fortune
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Demetrius the governor erected this temple of Fortune, feeling compassion for the city, like the son of Hierius he was. He built it on his own initiative, not the city’s, and at his own, not at the public expense.

poems.title: Book IX, 694: On an Arch
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The son of Messalinus built this magnificent arch.

poems.title: Book IX, 695: On the Stone Acoetonus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You see what great beauty lies in the disorderly order of the veins in the stone.

poems.title: Book IX, 696: On the Portico of the Basilica in Constantinople
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Theodorus, having built for the city four porticos, deserves to govern the city a fourth time.

poems.title: Book IX, 697: On another part of the same Portico
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: It beseemed thee, Theodorus, to adorn the columned temple of Fortune by such a wonderful work, and to give splendid gifts to Constantinople, city of the golden shield, which made thee consul and sees thee for the third time prefect.

poems.title: Book IX, 698: On the City of Mopsuestia
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You look on this famous city of Mopsus, which the seer once built, hanging its beauty over the river.

poems.title: Book IX, 699: On a Fountain called Olympias
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: From this fountain Alexander of Macedon drank splendid water, and said its streams were like his mother’s milk. Hence he named it Olympias, as this stone testifies.

poems.title: Book IX, 701: On the Temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This house is worthy of Zeus. Not even Olympus would blame Zeus for descending here from heaven.

poems.title: Book IX, 702: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The Athenians set up this house to Zeus, so that, descending from Olympus to earth, he might find another Olympus.

poems.title: Book IX, 703: An Extract from Herodotus (iv. 91)
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The sources of the river Tearus supply the best and most beautiful water of any river, and to these came, leading his army against Sardis, the most beautiful and best of all men, Darius, son of Hystaspes, king of Persia and all the continent.

poems.title: Book IX, 704: On a Rotunda
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Long time wears out even stone, but immortal is the renown of the good deeds of Asclepiodotus in giving so many and such splendid gifts to his native place. Now in addition to them all should be reckoned this hollow structure with its dome.

poems.title: Book IX, 705
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This gift, received from the city of Termessus in recognition of his upright jurisdiction, Eusebius dedicates to the god whose servant he is.

poems.title: Book IX, 710: On the Pyramids in Memphis
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Legend invented the false story of Ossa and Pelion mounted on Olympus. But even yet the Egyptian pyramids reach the golden Pleiads with their summits.

poems.title: Book IX, 713
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I am Myron’s little heifer, set up on a base. Goad me, herdsman, and drive me off to the herd.

poems.title: Book IX, 714
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Why, Myron, didst thou set me here by the altars ? Wilt thou not lead me into the house ?

poems.title: Book IX, 721a
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The cow has just returned from ploughing, and owing to that is lazy and will not advance.

poems.title: Book IX, 725
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Myron was looking for his own cow among the others, and found it with difficulty by driving the rest away.

poems.title: Book IX, 726
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The cow, its mother, moulded this heifer giving birth to it, but the hand of Myron did not mould it, but gave birth to it.

poems.title: Book IX, 727
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The horned cow would have spoken, though made of bronze, if Myron had worked entrails inside it.

poems.title: Book IX, 729
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Let someone attach me to the solid plough and put a yoke on my neck, for as far as depends on thy art, Myron, I will plough.

poems.title: Book IX, 731
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Myron placed me, the heifer, here, but the herdsmen throw stones at me thinking I have strayed.

poems.title: Book IX, 733
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Stranger, it was Myron who moulded this cow, on which this calf fawns as if it were alive, taking it for its mother.

poems.title: Book IX, 735
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A catr died beside thy heifer, Myron, deceived into thinking that the bronze had milk inside,

poems.title: Book IX, 736
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Alack! Myron, thou didst not have time to complete thy casting, but the bronze hardened before thou couldst put life into it.

poems.title: Book IX, 737
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou strikest the bronze heifer. Art deceived thee much, herdsman: Myron did not add life.

poems.title: Book IX, 741
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou wast bronze, deceptive heifer, and the husbandman came up to thee dragging a plough and carrying a yoke. He far excels all other artists, Myron, who by his labour made thee alive, just like a labouring cow.

poems.title: Book IX, 755: On Scylla in Bronze
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Unless the bronze glistened and betrayed the work to be a product of Hephaestus’ cunning art, one looking from afar would think that Scylla herself stood here, transferred from sea to land, so threatening is her gesture, such wrath does she exhibit, as if dashing ships to pieces in the sea!

poems.title: Book IX, 759
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Of one stone are chariot, charioteer, horses, yoke, reins, whip.

poems.title: Book IX, 760
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Of one stone are chariot, charioteer, horses, yoke, reins, and Victory.

poems.title: Book IX, 761: On a Painting of a Bunch of Grapes
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I was almost grasping the cluster in my fingers, more than deceived by the sight of the colours.

poems.title: Book IX, 779: On the Base of the Sun-dial in the Arch of the Basilica
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Look, Light of Freedom, on this gift of our emperor Justin, the tyrannicide, and his wife Sophia, this skilled bronze indicator of the hours from one to twelve. It had been stolen, and Julianus the Praetorian Prefect recovered it with incorruptible hands.

poems.title: Book IX, 780: On a Sun-dial
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is the learned stone which contains all the heavens, and which a little regulator adapts to every position of the sun.

poems.title: Book IX, 781: On the Lattice of a House
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: If you shut me I am open, and if you open me you will shut me. Being such, I cannot guard your house.

poems.title: Book IX, 783: On a Hermaphrodite which stood in a Bath
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To men I am Hermes, but to women appear to be Aphrodite, and I bear the tokens of both my parents. Therefore not inappropriately they put me, the Hermaphrodite, the child of doubtful sex, in a bath for both sexes.

poems.title: Book IX, 784: On a Small Bath
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Revile not small things. Small things possess charm. Cypris’ son, Eros, was small too.

poems.title: Book IX, 785: On a Vaulted Chamber on the West Side of the Forum
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Menas built the golden structure for all travellers, glorifying the city of our kings rich in gold.

poems.title: Book IX, 786
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The inhabitants erected to the god this beautiful altar, placing it here as a sign to mark the boundary of Leuce and Pteleus. The arbiter of the division is the king of the immortals himself, Cronus’ son.

poems.title: Book IX, 788
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Under thy rule, noble Fortune, the blest life of men enjoys the light of prosperity. For at thy nod all things bring glory to him whom thou permittest to caress thy divine neck with his right hand. To thy will illustrious kings bow, and the blest leaders of the learned company. Ships, too, rest safer in harbour, saved at sea by thy help, and cities enjoy tranquility, and peoples, and the ambrosial meads of the verdant plain. Therefore looking on thy servant...

poems.title: Book IX, 789: On a Rhetor
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Look on me, the adorner of learned discourse, who direct my art by the rule of eloquence.

poems.title: Book IX, 799: On the Porphyry Column in the Philadelphion
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Musenius is a well-wisher of the Emperor. Public works proclaim it; the force of facts is strong. He presented Constantinople with a Museum and with a splendid painting of the sovereign inside, an honour to poets, an ornament of the city, the hope of youth, the instrument of virtue, the wealth of good men.

poems.title: Book IX, 800: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: These works did Muselius cheerfully dedicate to words, in pure belief that God is the Word.

poems.title: Book IX, 801: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: He built parts of the Museum himself, and other parts which were in danger of falling he saved and set them up firmly.

poems.title: Book IX, 802: On a Portrait of the Emperor Marcian
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thou seest this shape, like a live horse, carrying Marcian, ruler of the race of men. His right hand is outstretched and he spurs on the galloping horse above a foeman, who seems to support its weight on his head.

poems.title: Book IX, 803: On a Portrait of the Empress Sophia at the Entrance of the Bath Leuxippus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Julian, the prefect of the city, dedicated here Sophia (Wisdom), the queen of the Italians, as being herself full of wisdom.

poems.title: Book IX, 804: On a Column with a Statue of the Emperor Justin
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Julian the prefect dutifully set up here the statue of Justin his master and benefactor.

poems.title: Book IX, 805: On a Stele of Ares partly buried in Thrace
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: As long as this fierce Ares rests on the ground the peoples of the Goths shall never set foot in Thrace.

poems.title: Book IX, 806: On a Sun-dial
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This place was once a garden, and the shade of the leaves shutting out the sun made it like night. But now Sergius, the patriarch, who hath seen with his eyes and reveals the mysteries of the Holy Trinity, contrived to make it bright and sunlit. Here this fixed stone seven times announces the eternal and fixed revolutions of the vault of heaven.

poems.title: Book IX, 807: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The mechanic art compels Phaethon by means of dials ruled in due measure to direct aright (?) the course of the sun. A small stone governs the circle of Aurora by its skilled division into hours and by the shadow’s mark. This work of mortals was constructed by the heavenly command of Sergius the patriarch.

poems.title: Book IX, 810
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is Justin next Sophia. Both made the golden work after their Assyrian triumph.

poems.title: Book IX, 811
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Justinian, the emperor, built me the bright house, a marvel for the sun to view at his rising. For never before when he mounted his celestial path did he see such beauty on earth.

poems.title: Book IX, 812: On Justin
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Domninus in the pure portals of Justice erected the statue of divine Justin, the pure guardian of Law.

poems.title: Book IX, 813: On Sophia his Wife
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This statue of Sophia stands before the gates of Justice, for wisdom should not be apart from justice.

poems.title: Book IX, 814: On a Bath
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Naiad Nymphs, ye truants, I never thought you would all quit my streams. But if the bath possesses such charm, Envy will accomplish naught, even though the Nymphs desert all the water.

poems.title: Book IX, 815: On Another
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Stranger, why dost thou quicken thy steps now, when thou seest the water that cures pain? This is the bath of joy; it washes away care, it lightens labour. It was built by Michael, the prefect of the Imperial Palace.

poems.title: Book IX, 816: On a Dish belonging to Eubulus
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: In presence of Telemachus and near Penelope, why, wise Odysseus, dost thou stretch out thy hand in terror? Thy nurse will never tell the suitors of thy gesture.

poems.title: Book IX, 817: On an Altar-cloth
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: On the table of the immaculate sacrifice I depict the passions of those sacrificed for Christ. For those whom I beg to have as protectors have I, Peter, put in the covering of the dread place.

poems.title: Book IX, 818: On a Disc
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I, another Peter, not having survived to see the life-giving tomb of the Lord, carved this disc representing the Holy Sepulchre, in which, bending low, I see Christ’s body.

poems.title: Book IX, 819: On a Cup
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I, the mystic cup, by the flow of the Holy Spirit pour into the heart a stream of repentance.

poems.title: Book IX, 820: On the Entrance of the Heraeum
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Justinian built this magnificent house, a thing of beauty to overhang land and water.

poems.title: Book IX, 821: On the Same
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Princes, Time will always proclaim your virtue, power, and great deeds, as long as the stars move in heaven.

poems.title: Book IX, 822: On a Dish with the Twelve Signs of the Zodiac
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is the silver heaven where the Moon gazes on the Sun, full herself of his reflected splendour, while on either side the fixed stars and the planets that move contrary to them work the whole fortune of the race of men.

poems.title: Book IX, 825: On a Machine for drawing Water which worked noiselessly, on which stood an image of Pan
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Echo fled from the waters, too, to escape me, Pan, her unhappy lover.

poems.title: Book IX, 125
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The brave Celts test their children in the jealous Rhine, and none regards himself as being the child’s father until he sees it washed by that venerated river. At once, when the babe has glided from its mother’s lap and sheds its first tears, the father himself lifts it up and places it on his shield, caring naught for its suffering; for he does not feel for it like a father until he sees it judged by the bath in the river, the test of conjugal fidelity. The mother, suffering new pangs added to those of childbirth, even though she knows him to be the child’s true father, awaits in fear and trembling the pronouncement of the inconstant stream.

poems.title: Book X, 3
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The way down to Hades is straight, whether you start from Athens or whether you betake yourself there, when dead, from Meroe. Let it not vex thee to die far from thy country. One fair wind to Hades blows from all lands.

poems.title: Book X, 9
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Ye fishermen, who pulled your little boat ashore here (Go, hang out your nets to dry) having had a haul of many sea-swimming gurnard (?) and scarus, not without (thrissa) honour me with slender first-fruits of a copious catch, the little Priapus under the lentise bush, the sea-blue god, the revealer of the fish your prey, established in this grove.

poems.title: Book X, 12
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Come and rest your limbs awhile, travellers, here under the juniper by Hermes, the guardian of the road—not a mixed crowd, but those of you whose knees ache from heavy toil and who thirst after accomplishing a long day’s journey. There is a breeze and a shady seat, and the fountain under the rock will still the weariness that weighs on your limbs. Escaping the midday breath of Autumn’s dog-star, honour Hermes of the wayside as is meet.

poems.title: Book X, 30
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Swift gratitude is sweetest ; if it delays, all gratitude is empty and should not even be called gratitude.

poems.title: Book X, 33
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: It is good to speak ever well of all; but to speak ill is a shame, even if men merit what we say.

poems.title: Book X, 38
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A time to love, and a time to wed, and a time to rest.

poems.title: Book X, 39
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A good friend, Heliodorus, is a great treasure to him who knows also how to keep him.

poems.title: Book X, 40
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Never give up the friend you have and seek another, listening to the words of worthless men.

poems.title: Book X, 43
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Six hours are most suitable for labour, and the four that follow, when set forth in letters, say to men “ Live.”

poems.title: Book X, 106
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Many are the thyrsus-bearers but few the initiated.

poems.title: Book X, 108
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Zeus the king, give us good things whether we pray for them or not, and keep evil things away from us even if we pray for them.

poems.title: Book X, 109
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Every word is vain that is not completed by deed, and let every deed spring from reason.

poems.title: Book X, 111
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Envy slays itself by its own arrows.

poems.title: Book X, 112
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Wine and baths and venerean indulgence make the road to Hades more precipitous.

poems.title: Book X, 113
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I do not wish or pray to be wealthy, but I would live on a little, suffering no evil.

poems.title: Book X, 114
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Below in Hell are judgment and Tantalus. I do not disbelieve it, realising by my poverty the infernal torments.

poems.title: Book X, 115
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Live by reason, and thou shalt not be in want.

poems.title: Book X, 116
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: “No married man but is tempest-tossed ”’ they all say and marry knowing it.

poems.title: Book X, 118
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: How was I born? Whence am I? Why came I here? To depart again? How can I learn aught, knowing nothing? I was nothing and was born; again I shall be as at first. Nothing and of no worth is the race of men. But serve me the merry fountain of Bacchus; for this is the antidote of ills.

poems.title: Book X, 119
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: To feed many slaves and erect many houses is the readiest road to poverty.

poems.title: Book X, 120
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Every woman loves more than a man loves; but out of shame she hides the sting of love, although she be mad for it.

poems.title: Book X, 124a
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Children are a trouble; it is a great evil if anything happens to them, and even if they live they are no small trouble. A wife if she be good hath something in her that delights, but a bad one brings a man a bitter life.

poems.title: Book X, 125
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A friend is a very difficult thing to find, but many or nearly all are friends only in name.

poems.title: Book X, 126
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: A useful servant is a good thing for him who makes use of him, but a man who is self-sufficient experiences less evil.

poems.title: Book XI, 3
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I would have liked to be as rich as Croesus once was, and to be king of great Asia. But when I look at Nicanor the coffin-maker and learn what these flute-cases he is making are meant for, I sprinkle my flour no matter where, and moistening it with my pint of wine I sell Asia for scent and garlands.

poems.title: Book XI, 8
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Bestow not scent and crowns on stone columns, nor set the fire ablaze ; the outlay is in vain, Give me gifts, if thou wilt, when I am alive, but by steeping ashes in wine thou wilt make mud, and the dead shall not drink thereof.’

poems.title: Book XI, 51
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Enjoy the season of thy prime ; all things soon decline: one summer turns a kid into a shaggy he-goat.

poems.title: Book XI, 52
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Caught, Thrasybulus, in the net of a boy’s love, thou gaspest like a dolphin on the beach, longing for the waves, and not even Perseus’ sickle is sharp enough to cut through the net that binds thee.

poems.title: Book XI, 53
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The rose blooms for a little season, and when that goes by-thou shalt find, if thou seekest, no rose, but a briar.

poems.title: Book XI, 56
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Drink and take thy delight ; for none knows what is to-morrow or what is the future. Hasten not and toil not ; be generous and give according to thy power, eat and let thy thoughts befit a mortal: there is no difference between living and not living. All life is such, a mere turn of the scale; all things are thine if thou art beforehand, but if thou diest, another’s, and thou hast nothing.

poems.title: Book XI, 86
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: No one knows if Pericles ran or sat in the stadion race. Marvellous slowness! “The noise of the barrier’s fall was in our ears” and another was receiving the crown and Pericles had not advanced an inch.

poems.title: Book XI, 102
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Thin little Diodorus once in taking a thorn out made a hole in the needle with his foot.

poems.title: Book XI, 108
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “(By some attributed to Julian the Apostate)”.
poems.text: Conon is two cubits tall, his wife four. In bed, then, with their feet on a level, reckon where Conon’s face is.

poems.title: Book XI, 109
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Little Demetrius has not wherewith to stoop, but always lies flat on the ground trying to get up.

poems.title: Book XI, 125
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The physician Crateas and the sexton Damon made a joint conspiracy. Damon sent the wrappings he stole from the grave-clothes to his dear Crateas to use as bandages and Crateas in return sent him all his patients to bury.

poems.title: Book XI, 126
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Charinus anointed my eye not with a spatula, but with a three-pronged fork, and he had a new sponge like those used for paintings. In pulling out the spatula he tore out my eye from the roots and the whole spatula remained inside. But if he anoints me twice, I shall not trouble him any more by suffering from sore eyes; for how can a man who no longer has eyes do so?

poems.title: Book XI, 145
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Sextus’ picture declaims, but Sextus is silent. The picture is a rhetor and the rhetor the image of his picture.

poems.title: Book XI, 149
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I see the very image of you, Medon the rhetor. Well, what is there surprising in that? You have arranged your dress effectively and you are silent. Nothing could be more like.

poems.title: Book XI, 151
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This is the image of a rhetor, but the rhetor is the image of his image. How is that? He does not speak. Nothing could be more life-like.

poems.title: Book XI, 158
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The wallet laments, and the fine sturdy Heracles club of Sinopian Diogenes and the double coat, foe of the cold clouds, befouled all over with encrusted dirt, lament likewise because they are polluted by thy shoulders. Verily I take Diogenes himself to be the dog of heaven, but thou art the dog that lies in the ashes. Put off, put off the arms that are not thine The work of lions is one thing, and that of bearded goats another.

poems.title: Book XI, 166
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: All say you are rich, but I say you are poor, for, Apollophanes, their use is the proof of riches. If you take your share of them, they are yours, but if you sayy them for your heirs, they are already someone else’s.

poems.title: Book XI, 182
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You are killing me, a pig but not your own, and ou call me “ piggie”’ (or “our own pig”), knowing well that I am not your own.

poems.title: Book XI, 193
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: What an evil is Envy but it has something good in it; for it wastes away the eyes and heart of the envious.

poems.title: Book XI, 198
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: “The nose’s Hermocrates ”—for if we say “ Hermocrates’ nose,” we give long things to little ones.

poems.title: Book XI, 202
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: After burying his old woman, Moschus very sensibly married a young girl, his first wife’s whole dowry remaining intact in his house. Moschus deserves to be praised for his good sense, in that he alone knows whom to sleep with and from whom to inherit.

poems.title: Book XI, 203
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Castor’s nose is a hoe for him when he digs anything, a trumpet when he snores and a grape-sickle at vintage time, an anchor on board ship, a plough when he is sowing, a fishing-hook for sailors, a flesh-hook for feasters, a pair of tongs for ship-builders, and for farmers a leek-slicer, an axe for carpenters and a handle for his door. Such a serviceable implement has Castor the luck to possess, wearing a nose adaptable for any work.

poems.title: Book XI, 219
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I don’t pay any attention, although some people are to be trusted; but in the meantime, for God’s sake, if you love me, Pamphilus, don’t kiss me.

poems.title: Book XI, 220
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Avoid the mouth of Alphaeus; he loves the bosom of Arethusa, falling headlong into the salt sea.

poems.title: Book XI, 244
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You bought a brass boiler, Heliodorus, colder than Thracian Boreas. Don’t blow the fire, don’t put yourself out; it is in vain you stir up the smoke. What you bought was a brass wine-cooler for summer.

poems.title: Book XI, 250
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The artist painted the fat man well, but to Hell with him if we shall look on two guzzlers instead of one.

poems.title: Book XI, 260
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: This Ouleuein you had long ago, but I don’t recognise the “b”’ (bouleuein, to be a senator), for it used to be written “d” (douleuein, to be a slave).

poems.title: Book XI, 261
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Parricius’ son is very well behaved, as he avoids all his fellows because of impure indulgence.

poems.title: Book XI, 262
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The young men of Alexandria bring down Selene divided in two in the ethereal night.

poems.title: Book XI, 267
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You, Mathematician, don’t require a measuring rod, and it is no concern of yours, for you have a nose three cubits long which no one grudges you.

poems.title: Book XI, 268
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Proclus cannot wipe his nose with his hand, for his arm is shorter than his nose; nor does he say “God preserve us” when he sneezes, for he can’t hear his nose, it is so far away from his ears.

poems.title: Book XI, 269
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I “victorious Heracles the son of Zeus’ am not Lucius but they compel me to be so.

poems.title: Book XI, 270
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “On a Statue of the Emperor Anastasius on the Euripus”.
poems.text: King, destroyer of the world, they set up this iron statue of thee as being much less precious than bronze, in return for the bloodshed, the fatal poverty and famine and wrath, by which thou destroyest all things owing to thy avarice.

poems.title: Book XI, 271
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Nigh to Scylla they set up cruel Charybdis, this savage ogre Anastasius. Fear in thy heart, Scylla, lest he devour thee too, turning a brazen goddess into small change.

poems.title: Book XI, 272
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: They denied their manhood and did not become women, nor were they born men, as they have suffered what women do; nor are they women, since a man’s nature was theirs. They are men to women and women to men.

poems.title: Book XI, 273
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Your mind is as lame as your foot, for truly your nature bears outside the image of what is inside.

poems.title: Book XI, 282
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I Lament no longer those who have left the sweet daylight, but those who ever live in expectation of death.

poems.title: Book XI, 297
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “On a Tippling Old Woman”.
poems.text: A, How is it, mother, that thou lovest wine more than me, thy son? Give me wine to drink since once thou didst give me milk. B. My son, my milk once stilled thy thirst, but now drink water and still thy own thirst.

poems.title: Book XI, 298
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: See how the son athirst reaches out his hand to his mother, and the woman, being a thorough woman, overcome by wine, drinking from a jar, spoke thus, looking askance: “ How shall I give thee to drink, my son, from a little droppie, for this jar holds but thirty pints.” “Mother, who hast rather the harsh nature of a step-mother, give me to quaff these tears of the sweetest vine.” “ Mother, evil mother, pitiless at heart, if thou lovest me, thy son, give me but a little to quaff.”

poems.title: Book XI, 316
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Milo the wrestler was once the only one who came to the sacred games, and the steward of the games called him to crown him at once. But as he was approaching he slipped and fell on his back, and the people called out: “Do not crown this man, as he got a fall when he was alone!”’ But he, standing up in their midst, shouted back: “ Are there not three falls? I fell once; now let someone give me the other two.”

poems.title: Book XI, 334
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Someone, hearing that “ Damagoras”’ and “ pestilence” were numerical equivalents, weighed the character of both from the beam of the balance. But the scale, when raised, was pulled down on Damagoras’ side, and he found pestilence lighter.

poems.title: Book XI, 335
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O unhappy Cynegirus, how among the living and in death art thou hacked by words and axes! Formerly thy hand fell fighting in the war, and now the grammarian has deprived thee of a foot.

poems.title: Book XI, 336
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Carinus, after receiving the spoils of Asia, set sail on a winter’s day at the setting of the Kids. Nemesis, too, saw the cargo, but he departed in her sight and laughing at the gods of the sea.

poems.title: Book XI, 337
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You are a senator, Agathinus, but tell me how much you paid now for the Beta, for formerly it was Delta.

poems.title: Book XI, 342
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You put the ruptured man’s rupture in front of him, he himself not being visible. Don’t present me to the rupture ; I want to see the man himself.

poems.title: Book XI, 343
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Silvanus has two servants, Wine and Sleep ; he no longer loves either the Muses or his friends, but the one flowing copiously into his head charms him from bed, and the other keeps him in his bedroom snoring.

poems.title: Book XI, 344
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “On Metrodotus, one of the Veneti! who had a Green Table”.
poems.text: Metrodotus, detesting the eternal burden of the Greens, has this table to keep him mindful of his hatred.

poems.title: Book XI, 345
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Metrophanes, swan-faced, shock-headed, lovely stork, shaking your head this way and that like a crane’s, you drag your long hood over the ground.

poems.title: Book XI, 356
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: The book of Homer, which never lies, lied about thee, saying the minds of young men are volatile.

poems.title: Book XI, 358
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Rurinianus was once Rufus in two syllables, but extended his syllables simultaneously with his crimes; but he does not escape the eye of two-syllabled Justice, for he shall again be called in two syllables Rufus the scoundrel and rascal, as he was before.

poems.title: Book XI, 359
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: O thou who art higher than all power, save my wretched self from all envy. Thou wouldest hear and I, too, would speak ; for the wish gives birth to double pleasure, while elegance on the speaker’s part and gravity on the hearer’s bestow double beauty on the speech. Thou art the luminary of speech and of laws, judging by law and excelling in speech. I saw in this prince a cat-like gold-grabber or a cruel leech, a mass of bile set in gold.

poems.title: Book XI, 360
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Now the general has become Hermanubis the dog, taking with him two brother Hermeses, stealers of silver, tied together with a rope, cold, prematurely dead demons of Tartarus. I know no place that accuses morals, but I say that morals accuse the place.

poems.title: Book XI, 411
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: You should call this not a bath but rather a funeral pyre such as Achilles lit for Patroclus, or Medea’s crown that the Fury set afire (?) in the bridal chamber of Glauce because of Jason. Spare me, bathman, for God’s sake, for I am a man who write all the deeds of men and gods. But if it is your purpose to burn numbers of us alive, light a wooden pyre, executioner, and not a stone one.

poems.title: Book XI, 415
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Who, Mentorides, so obviously transferred your breech to the place where your mouth formerly was? For you break wind and do not breathe, and you speak from the lower storey. I wonder how your lower parts became your upper !

poems.title: Book XI, 416
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Money comes into the hands of whores too. I care not. Let wretched gold that loves whores hate me. It is as difficult to get hold of me as to meet with a white crow.

poems.title: Book XI, 417
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “On an Elderly Woman annoying a Young Man”.
poems.text: Shake the acorns off another oak, Menesthion ; for I do not accept wrinkled apples past their season, but have ever desired fruit in its prime like myself; so why try to see a white crow?

poems.title: Book XI, 420
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: Your grey hairs, if you keep silent, are wisdom, but if you speak they are not wisdom but hairs, like those of youth.

poems.title: Book XI, 425
poems.author: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poems.text: I would have you know, Placianus, that every old woman with money is a rich coffin.

poems.title: Book XI, 426
